readings.head: {{RunningHeader|wang-tooth|6816|wanting}}
readings.c1s3:
''wank'', remove, change; OHG. ''wanchōn'', MHG. ''wanken'', be unsteady, vacillate, = Icel. ''vakka'' = Sw. ''vanka'', wander about; connected with AS. ''wincian'', etc., wink: see ''wink'', ''wince'', and cf. ''wench''.] Weak; unstable; not to be depended on. [North. Eng.]

'''wanly''' (won′li), ''adv.'' [< ''wan'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.] In a wan or pale manner; palely.

'''wanness''' (won′nes), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wannesse''; < ''wan''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness''.] The state or appearance of being wan; paleness; a sallow, dead, pale color: as, the ''wanness'' of the cheeks after a fever.

'''wannish''' (won′ish), ''a.'' [Early mod. E. also ''wanish''; < ''wan''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.] Somewhat wan; of a pale hue.
{{smaller block|The ''wanish'' moon, which sheens by night.
{{right|''Surrey'', Ps. viii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Upon her crest she wore a ''wannish'' fire,
Sprinkled with stars, like Ariadne’s tiar.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Lamia, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Morning arises stormy and pale,
No sun, but a ''wannish'' glare
In fold upon fold of hueless cloud.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, vi. 1.}}}}

'''wanrestful''' (won-rest′fu̇l), ''a.'' [< ''wan-'' + ''restful''.] Restless. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>An’ may they never learn the gaets
Of ither vile ''wanrestfu’'' pets.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Death of Poor Mailie.}}}}

'''wanrufe†''', ''n.'' [< ''wan-'' + Sc. ''rufe'', ''ruff'', ''roif'', rest; cf. ''roo''<sup>1</sup>.] Disquietude.
readings.c3s1:
'''4.''' To have occasion for, as something requisite, useful, or proper; require; need.
{{smaller block|<poem>Man ''wants'' but little here below,
Nor ''wants'' that little long.</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', The Hermit.}}
<poem>Not what we wish, but what we ''want'',
Oh! let thy grace supply. ''Merrick'', Hymn.</poem>}}
'''5.''' To feel a desire for; feel the need of; wish or long for; desire; crave.
{{smaller block|I ''want'' more uncles here to welcome me.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 1. 6.}}
The good pope . . . said, with scorn and indignation which well became him, that he ''wanted'' no such proselytes. ''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi.
If he ''want'' me, let him come to me.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}
'''6.''' To desire to see, speak to, or do business with; desire the presence or assistance of; desire or require to do something: as, you are the very man we ''want;'' call me if I am ''wanted;'' the general ''wanted'' him to capture the battery. ='''Syn.''' ''Need'', etc. See ''lack''<sup>1</sup>, ''v. t.''

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be lacking, deficient, or absent.
{{smaller block|<poem>If ye ''wanten'' in thees tweyne,
The world is lore.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Complaint to Pity, l. 76.}}
<poem>There shall ''want''
Nothing to express our shares in your delight, sir.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, iii. 1.}}
<poem>As in bodies, thus in souls, we find
What ''wants'' in blood and spirits, swell’d with wind.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Criticism, l. 208.}}}}
'''2.''' To fail; give out; fall short.

raw_text:
<noinclude><pagequality level="1" user="transcriber" />{{RunningHeader|wang-tooth|6816|wanting}}</noinclude><poem>Of this asses cheke, that was dreye,
Out of a ''wang-tooth'' sprang anon a welle.</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Chaucer'', Monk’s Tale, l. 54.}}}}

'''wangun''' (wâng′gun), ''n.''   [Amer. Ind.]   A place for keeping small supplies or a reserve stock; especially, the chest in a lumber-camp containing clothing, shoes, tobacco, etc., which are sold to the men.

'''wanhope†''' (won′hōp), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wanhope'' (= MD. ''wanhoop''); < ''wan-'' + ''hope''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' Lack of hope; hopelessness; despair.
{{smaller block|Thanne wex that shrewe in ''wanhope'' and walde haue hanged him-self.
{{right|''Piers Plowman'' (B), v. 286.}}}}
{{smaller block|Wel oughte I sterve in ''wanhope'' and distresse.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Knight’s Tale, l. 391.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Alle hise disciplis weren in ''wanhope'';
For to coumforte them ihesu thouȝte.</poem>
{{right|''Hymns to Virgin'', etc. (E. E. T. S.), p. 54.}}}}
'''2.''' Vain hope; delusion.
{{smaller block|The foolyshe ''wanhope'' . . . of some usurer.
{{right|''Chaloner'', tr. of Moriæ Encomium, H 3 b. (''Nares.'')}}}}

'''waniand†''', ''n.''   [ME. ''waniand'', ''wanyand'', ''wenyande''; appar. a noun use of ME. ''waniand'', ppr. (< AS. ''waniende'') of ''wanien'', ''wanen'', wane: see ''wane''<sup>1</sup>. Cf. ''wanion''.]   Waning; specifically, the waning of the moon, regarded as implying ill luck.
{{smaller block|<poem>Be they kyngis or knyghtis, in care ȝe thaim cast;
ȝaa, and welde tham in woo to wonne, in the ''wanyand''.</poem>
{{right|''York Plays'', p. 124.}}}}
{{smaller block|He would of lykelyhood bynde them to cartes and beate them, and make theym wed in the ''waniand''.
{{right|''Sir T. More'', Works, p. 306.}}}}

'''wanion†''' (wan′ion), ''n.''   [Also ''wannion'', ''wenion''; prob. a later form of ''waniand'', used in imprecations with a vague implication of ill luck or misfortune.]   A word found only in the phrases ''with a wanion'', ''in the wanion'', and ''wanions on you'', generally interpreted to denote some kind of imprecation.—'''With a wanion.''' {{smaller|(''a'') Bad luck to you; the mischief take you, or the like.}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Marry, hang you!
Westward ''with a wanion'' t’ ye!</poem>
{{right|''Marston, Jonson, and Chapman'', Eastward Ho, iii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|“Bide down, with a mischief to you—bide down ''with a wanion'',” cried the king.
{{right|''Scott'', Fortunes of Nigel.}}}}
{{smaller|(''b'') “With a vengeance”; energetically; vehemently; emphatically; hence, in short order; summarily.}}
{{smaller block|He should have been at home preaching in his diocese ''with a wannion.''
{{right|''Latimer'', 2d Sermon bef. Edw. VI., 1549.}}}}
{{smaller block|“Marry gep ''with a wenion!''” quod Arthur-a-Bland.
{{right|''Robin Hood and the Tanner'' (Child’s Ballads, V. 225).}}}}
{{smaller block|Yet considering with himself that wares would be welcome where money wanteth, he went ''with a wanion'' to his mother’s chamber, and there, seeking about for odd ends, at length found a little whistle of silver that his mother did use customarily to wear on.
{{right|''Harman'', Caveat for Cursetors, p. 76.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Come away, or I’ll fetch thee ''with a wanion.''</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Pericles, ii. 1. 17.}}}}
{{smaller block|I’ll tell Ralph a tale in ’s ear shall fetch him again ''with a wanion.''
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Knight of Burning Pestle, ii. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|I sent him out of my company ''with a wanion''—I would rather have a rifler on my perch than a false knave at my elbow.
{{right|''Scott'', Abbot.}}}}

'''wankapin''' (wong′ka-pin), ''n.''   [N. Amer. Ind.]   The water-chinkapin. Also ''yoncopin.''

'''wankle''' (wan′kl), ''a.''   [< ME. ''wankel'', < AS. ''wancol'', ''woncol'' (= OS. ''wancal'' = OHG. ''wanchal'', MHG. ''wankel''), unsteady, unstable; cf. OHG. MHG. ''wanc'', unsteady movement, doubt, G. ''wank'', remove, change; OHG. ''wanchōn'', MHG. ''wanken'', be unsteady, vacillate, = Icel. ''vakka'' = Sw. ''vanka'', wander about; connected with AS. ''wincian'', etc., wink: see ''wink'', ''wince'', and cf. ''wench''.]   Weak; unstable; not to be depended on. [North. Eng.]

'''wanly''' (won′li), ''adv.''   [< ''wan'' + ''-ly''<sup>1</sup>.]   In a wan or pale manner; palely.

'''wanness''' (won′nes), ''n.''   [< ME. ''wannesse''; < ''wan''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ness''.]   The state or appearance of being wan; paleness; a sallow, dead, pale color: as, the ''wanness'' of the cheeks after a fever.

'''wannish''' (won′ish), ''a.''   [Early mod. E. also ''wanish''; < ''wan''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ish''<sup>1</sup>.]   Somewhat wan; of a pale hue.
{{smaller block|The ''wanish'' moon, which sheens by night.
{{right|''Surrey'', Ps. viii.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Upon her crest she wore a ''wannish'' fire,
Sprinkled with stars, like Ariadne’s tiar.</poem>
{{right|''Keats'', Lamia, i.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Morning arises stormy and pale,
No sun, but a ''wannish'' glare
In fold upon fold of hueless cloud.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', Maud, vi. 1.}}}}

'''wanrestful''' (won-rest′fu̇l), ''a.''   [< ''wan-'' + ''restful''.]   Restless. [Scotch.]
{{smaller block|<poem>An’ may they never learn the gaets
Of ither vile ''wanrestfu’'' pets.</poem>
{{right|''Burns'', Death of Poor Mailie.}}}}

'''wanrufe†''', ''n.''   [< ''wan-'' + Sc. ''rufe'', ''ruff'', ''roif'', rest; cf. ''roo''<sup>1</sup>.]   Disquietude.
<poem>Bot I haif mervell in certaine
Quhat makis thé this ''wanrufe.''</poem>
{{smaller block|{{right|''Robene and Makyne'' (Child’s Ballads, IV. 246).}}}}

'''wanse†''' (wons), ''v. i.''   [Early mod. E. also ''wanze''; < ME. ''wansen'', diminish, decrease, < AS. ''wansian'', diminish; with verb-formative ''-s'', as in ''minsian'', decrease (see ''mince''), and ''clænsian'', cleanse (see ''cleanse''), < ''wan'', deficient: see ''wane''<sup>2</sup>.]   To wane; waste; pine; wither.
{{smaller block|<poem>His lively hue of white and red, his cheerfulness and strength,
And all the things that liked him did ''wanze'' away at length.</poem>
{{right|''Golding'', tr. of Ovid’s Metamorph., iii. (''Trench.'')}}}}

'''wanspeed†''', ''n.''   [ME. ''wanspede''; < AS. ''wanspēd''; as ''wan-'' + ''speed''.]   Ill fortune.
{{smaller block|What whylenes, or ''wanspede'', wryxles our mynd?
{{right|''Destruction of Troy'' (E. E. T. S.), l. 9327.}}}}

'''want<sup>1</sup>†''' (wont), ''a.''   [ME., also ''wont'', < Icel. ''vant'', neut. (with reg. Scand. neut. suffix ''-t'', as seen also in ''thwart'', another word of Scand. origin) of ''vanr'', lacking: see ''wan-'', ''wane''<sup>1</sup>.]   Lacking; deficient.
{{smaller block|And fyue ''wont'' of fyfty, quoth God, I schal forȝete alle.
{{right|''Alliterative Poems'' (ed. Morris), ii. 740.}}}}

'''want<sup>1</sup>''' (wônt), ''n.''   [< ME. ''want'', ''wonte'', lack, deficiency, indigence, < Icel. ''vant'', want, < ''vant'', lacking: see ''want''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.'']   '''1.''' Lack; deficiency; scarcity; dearth, or absence of what is needed or desired: as, ''want'' of thought; ''want'' of money.
{{smaller block|<poem>’Prentices in Paul’s Church-yard, that scented
Your ''want'' of Breton’s books.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wit without Money, iii. 4.}}}}
{{smaller block|He came the first Night to Mangera, but, for ''want'' of a Pilot, did not know where to look for the Town.
{{right|''Dampier'', Voyages, I. 125.}}}}

'''2.''' A vacant part, place, or space; a vacancy.
{{smaller block|The ''wants'' in the wheels of your watch are as useful to the motion as the nucks or solid parts.
{{right|''Baxter'', Divine Life, i. 10.}}}}

'''3.''' That which is lacking, but needed; the vacancy caused by the absence of some needful, important, or desirable thing.
{{smaller block|<poem>Yet, to supply the ripe ''wants'' of my friend,
I’ll break a custom.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', M. of V., i. 3. 64.}}}}

'''4.''' The state of being without means; poverty; penury; indigence.
{{smaller block|<poem>An endless Spring of Age the Good enjoy,
Where neither ''Want'' does pinch, nor Plenty cloy.</poem>
{{right|''Cowley'', Pindaric Odes, i. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Ring out the ''want'', the care, the sin,
The faithless coldness of the times.</poem>
{{right|''Tennyson'', In Memoriam, cvi.}}}}

'''5†.''' A time of need.
{{smaller block|He wept and shed many tears, blessing God that had brought him to see their faces, and admiring the things they had done in their ''wants''.
{{right|''N. Morton'', New England’s Memorial, p. 112.}}}}

'''6.''' That which cannot be dispensed with; a necessity.
{{smaller block|Habitual superfluities become actual ''wants''.
{{right|''Paley'', Mor. Phil., vi. 11.}}}}

'''7.''' In ''coal-mining'', same as ''nip''<sup>1</sup>, 8.—'''Want of consideration.''' {{smaller|See ''consideration''.}} ='''Syn. 1.''' {{smaller|Insufficiency, scantiness, dearth, default, failure.}}—'''3.''' {{smaller|Requirement, desideratum.}}—'''4.''' {{smaller|''Need'', ''Indigence'', etc. (see ''poverty''), distress, straits.}}

'''want'''<sup>1</sup> (wônt), ''v.''   [< ME. ''wanten'', ''wonten'', < Icel. ''vanta'', want, lack, < ''vanr'', neut. ''vant'', lacking: see ''want''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'']   '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To be without; be destitute of; lack: as, to ''want'' knowledge or judgment; to ''want'' food, clothing, or money. {{smaller block|<poem>Many a mayde, of which the name I ''want.''</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Parliament of Fowls, l. 287.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>The Lord our God ''wants'' neither Diligence,
Nor Love, nor Care, nor Powr, nor Providence.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas’s Weeks, i. 7.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>As a barren Coxcomb, that ''wants''
Discourse, is ever entertaining Company out of the last Book
He read in.</poem>
{{right|''Etherege'', She Would if she Could, iv. 2.}}}}
{{smaller block|They ''want'' many bad qualities which abound in the others.
{{right|''Swift'', Gulliver’s Travels, iii. 10.}}}}
'''2.''' To be deficient in; fall short in; be lacking in respect of, or to the amount of.
{{smaller block|Another will say it [the English language] ''wanteth'' Grammer. Nay, truly, it hath that praise, that it wanteth not Grammer: for Grammer it might have, but it needs it not.
{{right|''Sir P. Sidney'', Apol. for Poetrie (ed. Arber), p. 70.}}}}
{{smaller block|We ''want'' nothing now but one Dispatch more from Rome, and then the Marriage will be solemnized.
{{right|''Howell'', Letters, I. iii. 26.}}}}
{{smaller block|Trust me, Sir, I thought we had ''wanted'' three miles of this house, till you showed it to me.
{{right|''I. Walton'', Complete Angler, p. 56.}}}}
'''3.''' To do without; dispense with; spare.
{{smaller block|For law, physick, and divinitie need so the help of tonges and sciences as thei can not ''want'' them.
{{right|''Ascham'' (Ellis’s Lit. Letters, p. 16).}}}}
{{smaller block|Which they by this attempt were like to loose, and therefore were willing to ''want'' his presence.
{{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 58.}}}}
{{smaller block|The dragoons will be crying for ale, and they wunna ''want'' it, and maunna ''want'' it.
{{right|''Scott'', Old Mortality, iv.}}}} '''4.''' To have occasion for, as something requisite, useful, or proper; require; need.
{{smaller block|<poem>Man ''wants'' but little here below,
Nor ''wants'' that little long.</poem>
{{right|''Goldsmith'', The Hermit.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Not what we wish, but what we ''want'',
Oh! let thy grace supply. ''Merrick'', Hymn.</poem>}}
'''5.''' To feel a desire for; feel the need of; wish or long for; desire; crave.
{{smaller block|I ''want'' more uncles here to welcome me.
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. III., iii. 1. 6.}}}}
{{smaller block|The good pope . . . said, with scorn and indignation which well became him, that he ''wanted'' no such proselytes. ''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., vi.
If he ''want'' me, let him come to me.
{{right|''Tennyson'', Geraint.}}}}
'''6.''' To desire to see, speak to, or do business with; desire the presence or assistance of; desire or require to do something: as, you are the very man we ''want;'' call me if I am ''wanted;'' the general ''wanted'' him to capture the battery. ='''Syn.''' ''Need'', etc. See ''lack''<sup>1</sup>, ''v. t.''

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' '''1.''' To be lacking, deficient, or absent.
{{smaller block|<poem>If ye ''wanten'' in thees tweyne,
The world is lore.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Complaint to Pity, l. 76.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>There shall ''want''
Nothing to express our shares in your delight, sir.</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Thierry and Theodoret, iii. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>As in bodies, thus in souls, we find
What ''wants'' in blood and spirits, swell’d with wind.</poem>
{{right|''Pope'', Essay on Criticism, l. 208.}}}}
'''2.''' To fail; give out; fall short.

{{smaller block|They of the citie fought valiantly with Engines, Darts, Arrowes: and when Stones ''wanted'', they threw Siluer, especially molten Siluer. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 402.}}}}
{{smaller block|The front looking to the river, tho’ of rare worke for y<sup>e</sup> carving, yet ''wants'' of that magnificence which a plainer and truer designe would have contributed to it. {{right|''Evelyn'', Diary, Feb. 8, 1644.}}}}
'''3.''' To be in need; suffer from lack of something.
{{smaller block|He cannot ''want'' for money. {{right|''Shak.'', T. of A., iii. 2. 10.}}}}

'''want'''<sup>2</sup>† (wont), ''n.''   [Also ''wont;'' for ''wand'', < ME. ''wand'', < AS. ''wand'', a mole, also in comp. ''wandwyrp'', a mole (cf. ''moldwarp''), = G. dial. ''wond'', ''wonne'' = Sw. dial. ''vand'' = Norw. ''vand'', ''vaand'', ''vönd'', ''vond'', a mole.]   The mole or moldwarp.
{{smaller block|They found heards of deere feeding by thousands, and the Countrie full of strange Conies, headed like ours, vvith the feet of a ''Want'', and taile of a Cat, hauing vnder their chins a bagge, into which they gather their meat when they haue filled their bodie abroad. {{right|''Purchas'', Pilgrimage, p. 779.}}}}

'''want'''<sup>3</sup>†, ''n.''   [Prob. < Icel. ''vöttr'' (''vatt''-, orig. ''vant''-) = OSw. ''wante'', a glove, = Sw. Dan. ''vante'' = D. ''want'', a mitten; cf. OSw. ''winda'', wind, involve, wrap, = E. ''wind'', turn. Cf. OF. ''want'' (?), ''guant'', ''gant'', F. ''gant'' = Pr. ''gan'', ''guan'' = Sp. ''guante'' = Pg. ''guantes'' (pl.) = It. ''guanto'', prob. < ML. ''wantus'', a glove; < Teut. Hence (from the F. ''gant'') E. ''gantlet''<sup>2</sup>, ''gauntlet''<sup>2</sup>.]   A glove.   ''Imp. Dict.''

'''wa’n’t''' (wânt). A colloquial and vulgar contraction of ''was not''.

'''wantage''' (won′tāj), ''n.''   [< ''want''<sup>1</sup> + ''-age''.]   Deficiency; that which is wanting. {{smaller block|Inspectors and Gaugers shall make a detailed return (in duplicate) of each lot inspected, showing the serial number of each stamp affixed thereto, the gauge, ''wantage'', proof, and number of proof gallons.
{{right|''New York Produce Exchange Report'', 1888-9, p. 256.}}}}

'''wanter''' (wôn′tėr), ''n.''   [< ''want''<sup>1</sup> + ''-er''<sup>1</sup>.]   '''1.''' One who wants; one who is in need.
{{smaller block|The ''wanters'' are despised of God and men.
{{right|''Davies'', Scourge of Folly, p. 21. (''Davies.'')}}}}
'''2.''' An unmarried person who wants a mate.   ''Halliwell.'' [Colloq.]

'''want-grace†''' (wônt′grās), ''n.''   [< ''want''<sup>1</sup>, ''v.'', + obj. ''grace.'']   A reprobate.
{{smaller block|Want a ''want-grace'' to performe the deede.
{{right|''Davies'', Microcosmos, p. 57. (''Davies.'')}}}}

'''want-hill''' (wont′hil), ''n.''   [< ''want''<sup>2</sup> + ''hill''<sup>1</sup>.]   A mole-hill.
{{smaller block|Walter Eyres, digging ''want-hills'', 8s.
{{right|''Darrell Papers'' (in H. Hall’s Society in Elizabethan Age).}}}}

'''wan-thriven''' (won-thriv′n), ''a.''   [< ''wan-'' + ''thriven.'']   Stunted; decayed; in a state of decline. [Scotch.]

'''wanting''' (wôn′ting), ''p. a.''   [< ''want''<sup>1</sup> + ''-ing''<sup>2</sup>.]   '''1.''' Deficient or lacking.
{{smaller block|Thou art weighed in the balances, and art found ''wanting.'' {{right|Dan. v. 27.}}}}
{{smaller block|Each, with streaming Eyes, supplies his ''wanting'' Urn.
{{right|''Congreve'', Death of Queen Mary.}}}}
{{smaller block|The young people of our time are said to be ''wanting'' in reverence. {{right|''J. F. Clarke'', Self-Culture, p. 255.}}}}
'''2†.''' Needy; poor.
{{smaller block|<poem>You forget yourself:
I have not seen a gentleman so backward,
A ''wanting'' gentleman.</poem>
{{right|''Fletcher'', Wit without Money, ii. 4.}}}}<noinclude><references/></noinclude>
